parts.context: A brother and sister who run a small vegetable farm are dealing with an unexpected frost warning.

lines: Callum, have you looked at the forecast since lunch? The overnight low just dropped to minus three. Minus three, in the second week of September.
You’re joking. This morning it said plus four.

I know. A cold front is coming down much faster than they expected, and the skies are supposed to clear after midnight, which is the worst possible combination. No cloud cover, no wind. All the heat just escapes.
Okay, so what’s actually at risk? The squash will be fine, won’t it? The skins are already hard.

The winter squash, mostly yes, as long as it doesn’t get much colder than that. It’s the tomatoes and peppers I’m worried about. There’s still about half an acre of each out there, and a lot of it is only just starting to ripen. One hard frost and the whole lot turns to mush.
And that’s pretty much everything we were planning to sell at the market on Saturday.
Saturday and the restaurant. Chef Maalouf at the Larder ordered sixty kilos of heirloom tomatoes for their harvest dinner next Wednesday. That’s our biggest single order of the year.
Right. And of course this is the week Jesse decided to quit.
Don’t remind me. Without him it’s just you and me, and Mum still can’t lift anything with her back the way it is.
So, roughly, how much would we lose if we just let it go?
I did a quick count this morning. Between the market and the restaurant, somewhere around nine thousand dollars. That’s more than we made in the whole month of July.

qs.q: Why is the weather forecast especially worrying?
o: The frost will last for several nights in a row.
Calm, clear weather will make the frost more damaging.
The temperature will fall before sunset this evening.
The cold front will bring heavy rain along with the frost.
qs.ev: No cloud cover, no wind. All the heat just escapes
qs.x: Clear skies and no wind let the heat escape, making the frost worse. Nothing suggests several nights of frost; the sky clears after midnight, not before sunset.

qs.q: What does Rosalind say about the winter squash?
o: It needs to be harvested before anything else tonight.
It is what the restaurant ordered for its dinner.
It has already been picked and stored indoors.
It will probably cope with the expected cold.
qs.ev: The winter squash, mostly yes, as long as it doesn’t get much colder than that
qs.x: Its hard skins mean it should survive minus three. The restaurant ordered heirloom tomatoes, not squash.

qs.q: Why does Rosalind mention the month of July?
o: To emphasize how large the possible loss would be
To compare this year’s weather with the summer’s
To remind Callum when Jesse stopped working there
To explain when the restaurant placed its very large order
qs.ev: That’s more than we made in the whole month of July
qs.x: Comparing the $9,000 loss with a whole month’s income shows how serious it is. Jesse quit this week, not in July.

lines: Okay. What if we just pick everything tonight? Ripe or not. Green tomatoes ripen indoors, don’t they?

Some do, if they’ve started to turn colour. But think about it. Half an acre of tomatoes, half an acre of peppers, two people, and it gets dark at twenty past seven. We’d be lucky to get through a quarter of it.
Fair enough. What about the row covers? We used them in May for that late frost.
We’ve got enough fabric to cover maybe a third of the field. Not enough by a long way.
Or the sprinklers. Dad used to run them all night. The ice forms on the plants and somehow protects them.

It does work, in theory, but you have to keep the water running until the ice melts the next morning, and our well can’t keep up with that. Remember three years ago? The pump quit at four in the morning and we lost the entire cucumber crop. I’m not going through that again.
Okay, so no sprinklers. Then what about splitting it up? Covers on the most valuable stuff, and pick what we can of the rest.

That’s what I was coming round to. Peppers sell for nearly twice what tomatoes do per kilo, and the plants are lower to the ground, so the fabric goes much further. If we cover all the peppers, we’d still have a bit of fabric left over.

We pick every tomato that’s showing any colour, and we cover the heirloom rows for the restaurant with whatever fabric is left. The rest of the green ones, well, we’ll just have to take our chances with them.
It’s not perfect, but it’s a lot better than losing everything.

qs.q: Why does Rosalind reject harvesting everything tonight?
o: Green tomatoes cannot ripen once they are picked.
The vegetables would not sell well at the market.
There is too little time and help to finish the job.
Picking now would damage the plants needed for later harvests.
qs.ev: two people, and it gets dark at twenty past seven
qs.x: With only two workers and darkness at 7:20, they could pick about a quarter of the crop. She says some green tomatoes do ripen indoors, so the first option is wrong.

qs.q: How does Rosalind feel about using the sprinklers?
o: She refuses to risk repeating a past failure.
She doubts the method protects plants at all.
She would try it if their father were there to help.
She thinks it would use too much electricity overnight.
qs.ev: I’m not going through that again
qs.x: The pump failed three years ago and they lost the cucumbers, so she will not risk it again. She says the method “does work, in theory”, so she does not doubt it entirely.

qs.q: Why will the peppers be covered first?
o: They are more easily damaged by cold than tomatoes are.
The restaurant ordered peppers for its harvest dinner.
They were the crop that was covered in May.
They are worth more and are easier to cover.
qs.ev: Peppers sell for nearly twice what tomatoes do per kilo, and the plants are lower to the ground
qs.x: Peppers earn about twice as much and their low plants need less fabric. Row covers were used in May, but nothing says peppers were the crop covered then.

lines: Okay, we need more hands. I can call the Abernathy twins. They helped with the garlic in July, and they’re always looking for extra cash. I’ll text them to come over at six, after their shift at the arena.

Six is too late. If we’re covering and picking, we need to start by four at the latest, or we’ll be stretching fabric in the dark. Could you ask whether they can leave work early? Offer them an extra twenty dollars each if they can.
Will do. And what about the restaurant? If we lose some of the heirlooms tonight, we might not be able to deliver the full sixty kilos.

I’ll call Chef Maalouf this afternoon, before anything happens. I’d much rather warn her now and offer her something else, maybe some of the squash, or green tomatoes for a relish, than let her down on Wednesday morning.
Good idea. She raved about our squash last year, so she might even be pleased.
Let’s hope so. And Callum, set your alarm for five tomorrow. We need to pull the covers off by mid-morning, or the plants will cook underneath once the sun comes out.
Five a.m. Wonderful. Okay, I’ll go and dig the fabric and the clips out of the barn. Do you know where Dad put the big stakes?
Behind the tractor, I think. And grab the harvest bins while you’re there. We’ll need every single one of them tonight.

qs.q: What does Rosalind want Callum to do about the twins?
o: Text them to come over at six after work
Get them to arrive sooner by offering a bonus
Ask their parents whether they can help tonight
Pay them for the garlic harvest they did in July
qs.ev: Offer them an extra twenty dollars each if they can
qs.x: She wants them to leave work early and offers extra pay to make that happen. Six o’clock was Callum’s first plan, which she rejects as too late.

qs.q: Why does Rosalind want to call the chef this afternoon?
o: To ask her to collect the tomatoes earlier than planned
To cancel the order for the harvest dinner
To warn her early and propose substitutes
To raise the price of the heirloom tomatoes
qs.ev: I’d much rather warn her now and offer her something else
qs.x: She wants to give early notice and offer squash or green tomatoes instead. She does not cancel the order; she may simply be unable to deliver all sixty kilos.

parts.context: A customer is speaking with a technician at an appliance repair shop.

lines: Hi, I’m Hélène Lachance. Your technician came by yesterday to look at my fridge. He said someone would call, but I was driving past, so I thought I’d just drop in.

Of course, Ms. Lachance. I’ve got the report right here. So, on the phone you were told it was probably the start relay, which would have been an easy eighty-five-dollar fix. Unfortunately, once he had the back panel off, the relay was fine. The problem is the evaporator fan motor. That’s the fan that moves cold air from the freezer into the fridge section.
That explains why the freezer’s still frozen solid but the milk keeps going warm.

Exactly. The good news is that the compressor, which is the expensive part, is in great shape. The motor and labour together come to two hundred and forty dollars, and the repair comes with a ninety-day warranty.
Two-forty. Hmm. The fridge is nine years old. My brother-in-law says I’d be throwing good money after bad, and I should just buy a new one.

I hear that a lot. And sometimes it’s true. If it were the compressor, or if there were a refrigerant leak, I’d probably tell you the same thing. But a comparable new model is around sixteen hundred, plus delivery, and honestly, the newer ones aren’t built any better. A fan motor is a wear part. Replace it, and there’s no reason that fridge can’t give you another five or six years.
And the old one would just end up in a landfill, I suppose.
Well, the hydro utility does pick up old fridges for free and recycles them properly, so it wouldn’t be that bad. But keeping a working appliance running is still the greener choice.
Okay, you’ve convinced me. When can you do it?
The part has to come from the distributor. It should arrive by Thursday, and we could install it Thursday afternoon or Friday morning.
I’m at work all Friday morning, so Thursday afternoon is better. In the meantime, what do I do with my food?
Keep the fridge door closed as much as you can, and put the things that really need to stay cold, like milk and meat, in a cooler with some ice packs from the freezer.
I’ll manage. Thursday afternoon, then. Thanks for being straight with me.

qs.q: What was Ms. Lachance originally told on the phone?
o: That a small, inexpensive part had probably failed
That the evaporator fan would need to be replaced
That the compressor had developed a serious leak
That the technician would phone her the next morning
qs.ev: on the phone you were told it was probably the start relay, which would have been an easy eighty-five-dollar fix
qs.x: The phone diagnosis was the start relay, a cheap $85 fix. The fan motor was discovered only after the panel came off.

qs.q: Why does the technician think a repair makes sense?
o: The repair would cost less than delivering a new fridge.
New fridges are not available until next month.
The most costly component is still working well.
The fridge is still covered by the manufacturer’s warranty.
qs.ev: the compressor, which is the expensive part, is in great shape
qs.x: Because the compressor, the expensive part, is fine, a $240 repair is worthwhile. The ninety-day warranty belongs to the repair, not the manufacturer.

qs.q: What does the technician think of the brother-in-law’s advice?
o: It is correct, because the fridge is nine years old.
It ignores the cost of getting rid of an old fridge.
It is based on outdated information about prices.
It would suit some faults, but not this one.
qs.ev: If it were the compressor, or if there were a refrigerant leak, I’d probably tell you the same thing
qs.x: He agrees replacement can be right for compressor or refrigerant problems, but not for a fan motor. He never says the advice is correct for her fridge.

qs.q: What does the technician say about disposing of an old fridge?
o: It usually ends up in a landfill.
It can be collected and recycled at no cost.
It is picked up by the repair shop for a fee.
It must be delivered to the hydro utility.
qs.ev: the hydro utility does pick up old fridges for free and recycles them properly
qs.x: The utility picks old fridges up free of charge and recycles them. Landfill is Ms. Lachance’s assumption, which he corrects.

qs.q: When will the repair most likely be done?
o: On Friday morning, before she goes to work
As soon as the distributor calls the shop
On Thursday, later in the day
This afternoon, when she gets home
qs.ev: Thursday afternoon, then
qs.x: She chooses Thursday afternoon because she works on Friday morning. Friday morning was offered but rejected.

parts.context: A caller is getting information from a canoe outfitter before a backcountry trip.

lines: Hi, my friend and I are planning a four-night trip into Wolf Lake Provincial Park at the end of August, and I’d like to rent a canoe and some gear.

Great. Let me explain how it works. Canoes are forty-five dollars a day, but for trips of three days or longer, it drops to forty a day. We count each calendar day you have it, so if you pick it up on a Monday and return it on Friday, that’s five days, not four.
Oh, okay. So we’d be paying for five days, then.
Right. Paddles, life jackets and a bailer are included. We also take a two-hundred-dollar damage deposit on a credit card, which we release when the canoe comes back.
And the camping permits. Do you sell those?

We can, but most people buy them online through the park. Interior camping is fourteen dollars per person per night, and you have to choose your lake for each night when you book. The permit has to be printed, by the way. The rangers won’t accept one on your phone, because there’s no signal out there to check it.
Good to know. Is there anything we’re not allowed to bring?

No glass bottles or cans in the interior at all. Rangers do check, and the fine is a hundred and fifty dollars each. Repackage everything into plastic containers or bags. Also, food has to be stored in a bear-resistant barrel or hung at night. We include one barrel with every canoe rental.
One barrel for two people for five days. Will that be enough?
Honestly, it’ll be tight. Most pairs on a trip that long end up taking a second one. It’s an extra eight dollars a day.
You’ll need to filter or boil everything. We rent pump filters for six dollars a day, or you can buy purification tablets in our store.
And if we’re delayed, say by wind?

That’s important. When you return, you sign back in at our counter. If you’re not back by eight p.m. on your return date, we phone the emergency contact on your form and, after that, the park. So if you’re running late, there’s an emergency radio at the Wolf Lake ranger cabin, and you should use it. Late returns are also charged a full extra day.
Makes sense. Can we change our dates if the weather looks bad?
Up to seven days before pickup, free of charge. After that, we keep twenty-five percent of the rental.

qs.q: How much will Tariq pay to rent the canoe, not including extras?
qs.ev: So we’d be paying for five days, then
qs.x: Four nights means five calendar days, and trips of three days or more cost $40 a day, so $200. $225 uses the regular $45 rate, and $160 counts only four days.

qs.q: Why must the camping permit be printed?
o: Rangers cannot check digital permits in the park.
The park does not sell permits online any longer.
Printed permits show which lake was booked each night.
The outfitter needs a copy before releasing the canoe.
qs.ev: there’s no signal out there to check it
qs.x: With no signal, rangers cannot verify a permit on a phone. Permits are in fact sold online, so the second option contradicts her.

qs.q: What does Lucinda say about bringing canned drinks?
o: They must be packed inside the bear barrel.
Anyone found carrying them may be penalized.
They are allowed if they are carried back out.
They can be exchanged for plastic ones at the store.
qs.ev: Rangers do check, and the fine is a hundred and fifty dollars each
qs.x: Cans are banned, and rangers can fine people $150 each. The barrel is for food storage; cans are not allowed even if carried out.

qs.q: What does Lucinda suggest about the food barrel?
o: One barrel is the most a canoe can carry safely.
Two people rarely need more than the included one.
Extra barrels must be booked a week in advance.
Renting a second one would be a sensible idea.
qs.ev: Most pairs on a trip that long end up taking a second one
qs.x: By saying one will be “tight” and most pairs take two, she hints they should rent another. The one-week limit refers to free date changes, not barrels.

qs.q: What happens if the friends are not back by 8 p.m. on their return date?
o: The outfitter will start contacting people about them.
The park will send rangers to the ranger cabin.
Their damage deposit will be kept by the outfitter.
They must use the radio to request a free extension.
qs.ev: we phone the emergency contact on your form and, after that, the park
qs.x: The outfitter calls the emergency contact and then the park. Late returns cost an extra day, not the deposit, and the radio is for reporting delays, not for free extensions.

qs.q: How can the friends change their dates without paying?
o: By calling the shop on the day of pickup
By showing a forecast of strong winds
By paying twenty-five percent in advance
By making the change at least a week before pickup
qs.ev: Up to seven days before pickup, free of charge
qs.x: Changes are free up to seven days before pickup. Twenty-five percent is the charge for later changes, not a way to avoid paying.

parts.context: You will hear a news report about rising river levels.

lines: The Tamarack River is now expected to crest in Halden on Saturday morning, about a day earlier than forecast at the start of the week, after heavy rain combined with a late snowmelt upstream. The provincial river forecast centre predicts a peak about forty centimetres below the record set in 2011, but high enough to flood parts of the Riverside and Mill Creek neighbourhoods. The town has issued an evacuation alert, not yet an order, for about three hundred homes. That means residents should be ready to leave at short notice. Sandbag filling stations have opened at the arena and at the public works yard, and the town says it has delivered more than forty thousand bags so far. Emergency manager Shauna Pelletier says volunteers are welcome, but she’s asking people to register first rather than simply showing up.

On Wednesday, about two hundred people arrived at the arena at once, which was wonderful, but we had no way to organize them, and some streets got far more help than others. If you register online, we can send you exactly where you’re needed, and we can make sure the seniors on Mill Creek Road get help first.

Pelletier also urged residents in the alert area to move valuables and important documents upstairs, and to make a plan for their pets, since the reception centre at the high school can accept only cats and small dogs in carriers. Larger dogs can be boarded at the fairgrounds.
The other thing I’d stress is to stay off the river paths. Every year someone goes down to take a photo, and the banks are unstable right now. They can collapse without any warning.

Schools in Riverside will be closed on Friday, and the Second Avenue bridge will close at noon Friday as a precaution. The town says it will decide by Thursday evening whether to upgrade the alert to an order. Updates will be posted on the town’s website and broadcast on this station every hour until the river begins to fall.

qs.q: What has changed in the river forecast?
o: The river will now reach a record height.
The flooding will now affect fewer homes than expected.
Heavy rain is now expected to fall on Saturday.
The highest water will now arrive sooner.
qs.ev: about a day earlier than forecast at the start of the week
qs.x: The crest is now expected a day earlier. The peak is forty centimetres below the record, so the record option is wrong.

qs.q: What does the evacuation alert mean for residents?
o: They must leave their homes by Friday at noon.
They should be prepared to go at short notice.
They are required to register online with the town.
They should move to the reception centre tonight.
qs.ev: That means residents should be ready to leave at short notice
qs.x: An alert means getting ready to leave, not leaving yet. Noon Friday is when the bridge closes, and registering online is for volunteers.

qs.q: Why does Pelletier ask volunteers to register?
o: So that help can be shared out fairly and where it is most needed
So that the arena does not run out of sandbags
So that only experienced people work near the river
So that volunteers can be paid for their time
qs.ev: some streets got far more help than others
qs.x: Registration lets her send people where they are needed and prioritize seniors, after uneven help on Wednesday. Sandbag supply is never described as a problem.

qs.q: What is true about pets?
o: All pets can stay at the high school if kept in carriers.
Cats must be boarded at the fairgrounds this week.
Owners of large dogs will need to take them elsewhere.
Pets must remain upstairs in homes in the alert area.
qs.ev: Larger dogs can be boarded at the fairgrounds
qs.x: The high school takes only cats and small dogs, so large dogs must go to the fairgrounds. Valuables, not pets, are to be moved upstairs.

qs.q: What will the town decide by Thursday evening?
o: Whether to close the Second Avenue bridge
Whether residents will be required to leave
Whether schools in Riverside will reopen
Whether to open more sandbag stations
qs.ev: whether to upgrade the alert to an order
qs.x: Upgrading to an order would make leaving mandatory. The bridge closure and school closures have already been decided.

parts.context: Three members of a condominium board are deciding what to do about the building’s roof.

lines: Right, the main item tonight. The engineer’s report confirms what we suspected: the roof membrane has maybe two years left, and he recommends replacing it next summer. Our reserve fund has a hundred and ninety thousand set aside for exactly that. The question is what kind of roof we put on. Femi, you’ve been pushing for solar.

I have. If we’re taking the roof off anyway, this is the moment to do it. A sixty-panel system would cover most of the electricity in the common areas: hallways, the elevator, the parking garage lights. The installer estimates it would pay for itself in about eleven years.
Eleven years. And how much does it cost?
About a hundred and forty thousand, on top of the membrane.
So we’d need a special assessment. That’s roughly two thousand dollars per unit. I can already hear the complaints at the annual meeting. Half our owners are retirees on fixed incomes.
That was my worry too. What about the green roof idea, Hiroshi? You raised it last month.

I did, and I still like it in principle. Plants absorb rainwater, they keep the top floor cooler, and it would look lovely from the units on the north side. But I’ve done some reading since then, and the engineer was pretty clear. Our structure wasn’t designed for that kind of weight. We’d need reinforcement, and that alone could double the cost. So I’ve dropped it, reluctantly.
Thank you for saying that. Honestly, I think solar is the only option that actually saves money.

There’s a third option the engineer mentioned that nobody’s talked about: a white reflective membrane. It costs about eight percent more than a standard black one, but it reflects most of the sun’s heat. He thinks the top-floor units could see their summer cooling costs drop by a fifth or more.
Eight percent more on a hundred and ninety thousand, that’s around fifteen thousand. We could cover that from the reserve without an assessment.
Sure, but it isn’t generating anything. It’s just less bad.

That’s fair. But here’s a thought. The engineer said that if we install the mounting brackets for solar panels now, while the roof is open, it costs about twelve thousand. Then we could add panels later without cutting into the new membrane.
Exactly. And the province has a community energy grant that opens in the spring. If we got it, it could cover up to forty percent of the panels.
I could support that. White membrane plus brackets is twenty-seven thousand or so extra, all from the reserve, no assessment. Then the owners vote on the panels once we know about the grant.
I’ll be honest, I’d rather do it all at once. Every year we wait is another year of electricity bills. But I can count votes, and I’d rather get solar in two steps than not at all.
Good. So the motion is: white reflective membrane and solar mounting brackets, funded from the reserve. Femi, would you be willing to prepare the grant application?
Happy to. I’ll need the last two years of electricity bills from the management company, though.
I’ll ask them for those tomorrow. And I’ll write up a one-page summary for owners, so nobody hears about it through rumours first.
Perfect. I’ll put the motion to a vote at the next meeting.

qs.q: What does the engineer’s report say about the roof?
o: It will need replacing in the fairly near future.
It could last much longer if it is repaired next summer.
It is strong enough to carry a heavier green roof.
It should be replaced only after the reserve fund grows.
qs.ev: the roof membrane has maybe two years left
qs.x: With about two years left, it must be replaced soon, next summer. The engineer said the structure cannot carry a green roof’s weight.

qs.q: Why is Hiroshi worried about Femi’s solar proposal?
o: The panels would not pay for themselves for eleven years.
The roof could not support sixty solar panels.
Owners with limited incomes would face an extra charge.
The installer’s estimate seemed unrealistically low.
qs.ev: Half our owners are retirees on fixed incomes
qs.x: A $2,000 special assessment would hit retirees on fixed incomes. He asks about the eleven-year payback but objects to the cost per unit.

qs.q: How does Hiroshi now feel about the green roof?
o: He thinks it would be cheaper than solar panels.
He wants to raise it again at the annual meeting.
He believes the engineer misunderstood the idea.
He still likes it but accepts it is not practical.
qs.ev: So I’ve dropped it, reluctantly
qs.x: He still likes it “in principle” but dropped it because of the building’s structure. He agrees with the engineer rather than doubting him.

qs.q: What benefit of the white membrane does Bernadette mention?
o: It costs the same as a standard black membrane.
It could lower summer cooling bills on the top floor.
It would produce power for the parking garage.
It qualifies the building for a provincial grant.
qs.ev: the top-floor units could see their summer cooling costs drop by a fifth or more
qs.x: It reflects heat, cutting top-floor cooling costs. It costs about eight percent more than a black membrane, and the grant is for solar panels.

qs.q: What is Femi’s attitude toward the white membrane?
o: He thinks it should be paid for with a grant.
He considers it the best option the board has.
He believes it costs far more than Hiroshi claims.
He sees it as an improvement but not a real solution.
qs.ev: It’s just less bad
qs.x: “Just less bad” means it helps a little but produces nothing, so it is not a real solution for him. He still prefers solar.

qs.q: Why does Bernadette suggest installing the mounting brackets now?
o: Panels could be added later without damaging the new roof.
The brackets are cheaper than the white membrane.
The grant will only pay for buildings with brackets.
The installer has offered a discount until next summer.
qs.ev: Then we could add panels later without cutting into the new membrane
qs.x: Brackets fitted while the roof is open let panels go on later without cutting the new membrane. No condition about brackets is attached to the grant.

qs.q: Why does Femi accept the final plan?
o: He agrees the payback period is too long.
He thinks the grant will cover most of the cost.
He prefers partial progress to losing the vote.
He was persuaded by the cooling savings.
qs.ev: I’d rather get solar in two steps than not at all
qs.x: He knows the votes are not there for full solar now, so he accepts a two-step approach. The grant would cover up to forty percent, not most of the cost.

qs.q: What will Hiroshi do next?
o: Prepare the application for the energy grant
Request records from the management company
Present the motion at the next meeting
Collect owners’ opinions on solar panels
qs.ev: I’ll ask them for those tomorrow
qs.x: Hiroshi will ask the management company for the electricity bills. Femi prepares the grant application, and Bernadette presents the motion.

parts.context: A reporter presents different views on a plan to use planned burns to reduce wildfire risk near a small town.

lines: On the hillsides above Spruce Hollow, the forest is unusually thick. Decades of putting out every fire, even small ones, have allowed dead wood and young trees to build up on the forest floor, and many experts now describe the area as fuel waiting for a spark. This fall, the provincial wildfire service wants to do something that alarms some residents: set fires on purpose. The plan calls for a series of prescribed burns covering about six hundred hectares over three years, carried out only on days when wind, humidity and temperature fall within strict limits. A fire ecologist with the wildfire service told me the goal isn’t to burn the forest down, but to burn the right things at the right time. Low-intensity fires clear out small trees and dry debris while leaving the large trees standing. She points to research showing that when wildfires later reached treated areas, they slowed down and dropped to the ground, giving crews a chance to stop them. Without the burns, she said, the question isn’t whether Spruce Hollow faces a major fire, but when. Not everyone is convinced. Wade runs a bed-and-breakfast on the edge of town, and he remembers a planned burn in another province that escaped its boundaries.

They tell you it’s under control, and ninety-nine times out of a hundred it probably is. But I’ve got my life savings in this place. If it’s the hundredth time, who pays for that? And even if nothing goes wrong, the smoke sits in the valley for days. September and October are my busiest months, with all the fall-colour tourists. I’d lose bookings.

The wildfire service says escapes are extremely rare, and that burns would be scheduled to avoid long weekends where possible. Wade says he’d feel better if the province offered compensation for lost business, something officials say isn’t currently on the table. Health professionals raise another concern. A respiratory therapist at the regional hospital told me that some of her patients with lung disease are already anxious about the plan. But she sees it differently than you might expect. In her view, a few days of light, managed smoke, announced in advance, is far easier to prepare for than weeks of thick smoke from an uncontrolled wildfire. What she wants is advance notice of at least seventy-two hours, so vulnerable patients can make arrangements or leave town for a few days. Council will hold a public information session next month before the first burn is approved, and the wildfire service says it will publish maps of every planned burn area ahead of that meeting.
Look, I’m not against it, exactly. I just want someone to look me in the eye and tell me who’s responsible if it goes wrong.

qs.q: According to the report, why has the forest near Spruce Hollow become dangerous?
o: Planned burns in the past were poorly controlled.
Dry summers have killed many of the largest trees.
Past fire prevention let flammable material accumulate.
Tourists have left debris on the forest floor.
qs.ev: Decades of putting out every fire, even small ones, have allowed dead wood and young trees to build up
qs.x: Putting out every fire allowed dead wood and young trees to pile up. The escaped burn Wade mentions happened in another province, not near Spruce Hollow.

qs.q: What is the fire ecologist’s main point?
o: Large trees must be removed to protect the town.
Burns should be avoided during the tourist season.
A major wildfire near the town is very unlikely.
Controlled fires make later wildfires easier to fight.

p1.meta: From: Fergus Doyle | To: Amaya Solís | Subject: Greetings from the cabin – and an invitation
p1.text:
Dear Amaya,

It’s been almost a year since I traded my desk at the planning office for a cabin forty minutes outside Whitehorse, and I’ve finally got enough battery power to sit down and write you a proper email.

Living off the grid has turned out to be both easier and harder than I imagined. The solar panels I installed last spring produce more electricity than I can use from May to August, when the sun barely sets. In December, though, we get about six hours of weak daylight, and the panels are often buried in snow. I spend a surprising number of mornings on a ladder with a broom. For the darkest weeks, I rely on a small generator, which I hate running, partly because of the noise and partly because it feels like cheating.

Heating has been the bigger lesson. I assumed the wood stove would be the easy part, but I badly underestimated how much firewood I’d need. I burned through my entire supply by the end of January and had to buy two more cords at a painful price from a neighbour. This year I started cutting and stacking in June, and the woodpile now reaches the eaves.

What I didn’t expect is how much I’d love the quiet. Some nights the northern lights are so bright I can read by them – well, almost. My neighbours, the nearest of whom lives two kilometres away, have been incredibly generous, and I’ve learned more practical skills in twelve months than in the previous twenty years.

Now, the real reason I’m writing. You mentioned last summer that you’d love to visit, and I’d love to have you. Most people would tell you to come in July, and you’d certainly be more comfortable. But if you want to see the aurora properly, February or early March is ideal. It can be minus thirty, and the outhouse is, let’s say, an adventure. I’d understand completely if you’d rather wait for summer.

Let me know what you think, and whether your knee would cope with snowshoeing.

Warmly,
Fergus

p3.title: Borrowing Seeds: The Rise of Seed Libraries
paras: Walk into a growing number of public libraries in Canada and, next to the new releases, you may find an old wooden card catalogue filled not with index cards but with envelopes of seeds. The idea behind a seed library is simple. Gardeners “borrow” seeds in the spring, grow them over the summer, then allow a few of their best plants to go to seed and return a portion of the harvest in the fall. In theory, the collection replenishes itself and even grows each year. Most seed libraries are free and require nothing more than a library card. Organizers say the appeal goes beyond saving money. Many borrowers are beginners who would never spend twenty dollars on seed packets for a hobby they might abandon, and a free envelope of beans lowers the risk of trying.

In practice, running a seed library involves more than filling drawers. Volunteers spend hours sorting donations, labelling envelopes and checking that seeds are dry and free of mould. Not all plants are equally suitable. Beans, peas, lettuce and tomatoes are popular because they mostly pollinate themselves, so the seeds they produce grow into plants like the parent. Squash and cucumbers are trickier: grown near other varieties, they cross easily, and a gardener who saves seeds from a prize pumpkin may get something strange and inedible the following year. For this reason, many libraries label seeds by difficulty and recommend that beginners start with the easy group. Some also hold seed-saving workshops in late summer, which coordinators say are now among the best-attended events on their calendars.

Supporters argue that seed libraries do something commercial catalogues cannot: they build up varieties suited to local conditions. A tomato whose seeds have been saved for ten years in a short Prairie summer is gradually selected for plants that ripen early and tolerate cool nights. Collections also preserve family heirlooms. In one Manitoba library, the most requested item is a speckled bean donated by a family who brought it from Ukraine more than a century ago. Each envelope carries a short note about its history, and borrowers often say the stories are half the attraction. For the library, these donations can be irreplaceable, since many of the varieties are not sold anywhere, and if the last gardener growing them stops, the variety disappears.

The biggest challenge, coordinators admit, is getting seeds back. Surveys at several libraries suggest that only a minority of borrowers ever return seeds, often because their plants failed, or because they simply forgot. Most libraries respond with patience rather than penalties, since the goal is to encourage gardening, not to police it. To keep collections stocked, they rely on donations from experienced gardeners and local farms, and some top up with purchased seed each spring. Funding is usually modest, coming from library budgets or small community grants. Even so, coordinators say demand keeps rising. Several libraries now run out of popular varieties, such as cherry tomatoes and snap peas, within weeks of opening the drawers in March. Some have started limiting borrowers to five envelopes each so that latecomers are not left empty-handed.

p4.title: It’s Time to Put Out the Urban Wood Fire
p4.byline: Opinion | by Malcolm Achterberg, environmental health researcher
p4.text:
Few things feel more Canadian than a crackling fire on a January evening. I understand the appeal; I grew up in a house with a wood stove, and the smell of birch smoke still reminds me of my grandmother’s kitchen. But nostalgia should not stop us from facing an uncomfortable fact: in many Canadian cities, residential wood burning is now one of the largest sources of fine particle pollution in winter.

The particles in wood smoke are tiny enough to travel deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. They are linked to asthma attacks, heart disease and premature death. On cold, still nights, especially in valleys, a layer of warm air can trap smoke close to the ground for days. A single old fireplace can release more fine particles in an evening than dozens of modern cars driving for the same period. And unlike traffic, wood smoke does not stay on the street. It seeps into neighbouring homes through windows, vents and gaps around doors.

This is not a problem that falls evenly. The people who suffer most are often those who did not light the fire: the child with asthma next door, the elderly neighbour with heart problems, the family who cannot afford an air purifier. Burning wood in a city is, in effect, a decision about what other people will breathe.

I am not proposing that we confiscate anyone’s stove. Rural households, where wood is often the main or only source of heat, face a very different situation, and many depend on it during power outages. Nor do I think that a modern certified stove, burning dry wood, is in the same category as an open fireplace with a smouldering, damp log.

What I am proposing for urban areas is a set of reasonable, gradual steps. First, cities should prohibit all recreational burning on days when an air quality advisory is in effect, with exemptions for homes that have no other source of heat. Several municipalities already do this, and compliance has been better than critics predicted. Second, any new wood-burning appliance installed in a city should meet current emission standards. Third, and most ambitiously, uncertified fireplaces and stoves should be removed or replaced when a home is sold, with a modest incentive to help owners switch to a cleaner option.

Some readers will object that this is government reaching into the living room. I would answer that we already accept rules about what we can burn in our backyards, how loud our parties can be and how fast we drive past schools. Each of those rules exists because one person’s choice affects someone else’s health or safety. Wood smoke belongs on that list.

Others will say that the contribution of a few fireplaces is too small to matter. The data say otherwise. In cities where restrictions on burning during advisories have been introduced, winter particle levels have dropped noticeably within a few years.

A fire in the hearth can be a genuine comfort. But comfort for one household should not come at the cost of another family’s health. It is time for our cities to treat wood smoke as the pollutant it is.

t1.situation: Last weekend you took a guided sea kayaking tour with a company called Tidewater Paddle Tours. During the trip, the weather changed, and you felt that the guide did not handle the situation safely. Write an email to the company’s manager.
bullets: Describe what happened during the tour
Explain why you felt the situation was unsafe
Say what you would like the company to do
t1.model:
Dear Manager,

I am writing about the three-hour sea kayaking tour I took with Tidewater Paddle Tours last Saturday, which left the harbour at 1:00 p.m. with eight participants and one guide.

About an hour into the trip, the wind picked up sharply and the waves became much rougher. Several of us asked to turn back, but the guide insisted on continuing to the island so that we could “get our money’s worth”. On the way, one participant, an older man, capsized. Because the guide was at the front of the group, it took nearly ten minutes for him to reach the man, who was very cold and frightened by the time he was helped back into his kayak.

I felt unsafe for several reasons. Most of us were beginners, there was only one guide for eight paddlers, and the weather warning had been posted before we even launched.

I would like the company to review its policy on ratios and weather decisions, and I believe a partial refund would be fair. I would appreciate a response within two weeks.

Sincerely,
Priyamvada Nair

t2.intro: Your town has received money to create a winter skating area in its central park. It can afford only one of the following options.
t2.question: Which option do you prefer?
t2.a: Build a refrigerated outdoor rink with lighting, boards and a warming hut. It would stay open from late November to mid-March regardless of the weather, but would use a significant amount of electricity.
t2.b: Restore the park’s natural pond, adding a skating trail around its edge and planting native trees. Skating would depend on the weather, but the pond would also provide habitat for birds and frogs all year.
t2.model:
I would choose Option B, restoring the natural pond, even though I know it means accepting some uncertainty about the skating season.

First, this option offers value all year rather than only in winter. A refrigerated rink sits empty and fenced for eight months, but a healthy pond surrounded by native trees would attract birds, frogs and dragonflies, and give families a peaceful place to walk in every season. Teachers could even bring classes there for nature lessons.

Second, I am concerned about the running costs of a refrigerated rink. Keeping ice frozen when it is several degrees above zero requires a great deal of electricity, and the town would be paying those bills for decades. That money could support other programs instead.

Of course, the main drawback of the pond is that some winters will be too mild for safe skating. However, a skating trail through the trees would be a magical experience on the weeks when it does freeze, and the town could still flood a small temporary rink on the tennis courts as a backup. Overall, the pond is the more sustainable and versatile choice.

t1.prompt: Your friend lives in a downtown apartment with a small balcony and wants to start growing vegetables this summer. They have never grown anything before. Give your friend some advice about how to get started.
t1.model: That’s such a fun project, and you really don’t need much space to grow a surprising amount of food. My first piece of advice is to watch your balcony for a few days and figure out how much sun it actually gets. Most vegetables, like tomatoes and peppers, need at least six hours of direct sunlight. If your balcony only gets morning sun, you’d be better off with lettuce, spinach and herbs, which are happier in partial shade. Second, start small. It’s tempting to buy ten different plants, but I’d begin with three or four big containers. Pick easy crops, like cherry tomatoes, bush beans and basil, so you get some early success and don’t get discouraged. Also, buy proper potting mix, not garden soil, because garden soil gets hard and doesn’t drain well in pots. Third, think about water. Containers dry out really quickly in the heat, so you might need to water every day in July. A self-watering pot or a simple drip tray can save you a lot of stress, especially if you go away for a weekend. Finally, check your building’s rules about weight and dripping water, so you don’t end up in trouble with your neighbours downstairs.

t2.prompt: Talk about a time when you saw a wild animal up close. What happened, and how did you feel?
t2.model: A couple of years ago, I was hiking with my brother in the mountains, and we stopped at a small lake for lunch. While we were eating, we heard something splashing, and when we looked up, there was a moose standing in the water, maybe thirty metres away. It was a female with a young calf behind her. At first I was thrilled. She was enormous, much bigger than I expected, and she just kept eating plants from the bottom of the lake. But then she lifted her head and stared straight at us, and her ears went back. My brother whispered that mothers with calves can be dangerous, so we quietly packed up and backed away along the trail. My heart was pounding the whole time. Looking back, it was one of the most amazing moments I’ve had outdoors, but it also taught me to respect wildlife from a distance.

On the left, a woman in a yellow shirt and a sun hat carries a bag and bends toward the sand. A boy in an orange shirt carries a small box full of litter. In the centre, a man in a green shirt stands at a folding table with a clipboard-style book, handing out supplies, and there are two bins next to the table, a blue one labelled RECYCLING and a grey one labelled GARBAGE. On the right, a beach umbrella shades a towel, a woman in a red shirt is pointing toward the water, and a brown dog is running along the shore. A small white boat is out on the water.

t3.prompt: Describe some things that are happening in the picture as well as you can. The person you are speaking to cannot see the picture.
t3.model: This picture shows a beach clean-up event on a sunny morning. Across the top, there’s a big blue banner that says Beach Clean-up Day. On the left, a woman in a yellow T-shirt and a wide sun hat is carrying a bag, and she seems to be picking up litter from the sand. Next to her, a young boy in an orange shirt is carrying a box that’s probably full of garbage he’s collected. In the middle, a man with glasses in a green shirt is standing behind a folding table, maybe signing people in or handing out supplies. Beside the table there are two bins, a blue one for recycling and a grey one for garbage. On the right, there’s a red beach umbrella over a purple towel, and a woman in a red top is pointing toward the water. A brown dog is running along the shore, and there’s a small white boat out on the lake.

t4.prompt: In this picture, what do you think will most probably happen next?
t4.model: I think the woman in the red top has probably spotted some garbage floating near the shore, so she’ll likely call the volunteers over to help pull it out. The man at the table will probably hand out gloves or another bag, and a couple of people will wade in to grab it. Meanwhile, the brown dog is running loose along the beach, and I suspect it’s going to find something interesting in the sand, maybe an old food wrapper, and run off with it. The little boy will probably chase after the dog to get the litter back, which could be pretty funny to watch. Later on, once the bins fill up, I imagine the organizers will weigh the bags or count how much they collected, and then everyone will gather under the banner for a group photo to share on the community page.

t5.intro: Your extended family is planning a reunion weekend next August and has narrowed the location down to a few choices. Choose the option that you prefer. In the next section, you will need to persuade a family member that your choice is better than the one they prefer.

options.title: Provincial park group campsite
details: $480 for the weekend, up to 40 people

options.title: Farm guesthouse
details: Sleeps 22 indoors; others in a nearby motel
Farm animals and hay rides for kids

other.title: Lakeside resort
details: Pool, tennis courts and boat rentals

t5.persuade: Your uncle prefers the lakeside resort. Persuade your uncle that your choice is better.
t5.model: I know the resort looks really comfortable, Uncle Ray, but I think the farm guesthouse is a much better fit for our family. First, think about the cost. The resort is thirty-six hundred dollars, almost double the farm, and that’s before anyone pays for boat rentals or restaurant meals. With so many cousins still in university, I’d hate for anyone to skip the reunion because of money. Second, the drive. Four hours each way with little kids and Grandma is a lot, and the farm is only two. And honestly, a reunion is about spending time together. At a resort, everyone scatters to their own cabins, the pool or the tennis courts. At the farm, most of us would be under one roof, the kids would have the animals and hay rides, and the Saturday dinner is already included, so nobody spends the evening cooking. It feels much more like family.

t6.situation: Your 17-year-old nephew and two friends are planning a four-day backcountry hiking trip next week, during a hot, dry summer. A wildfire is burning about 80 kilometres from their route, and a campfire ban has just been announced. Your sister, his mother, has already given permission, but you are worried.
options: Talk to your nephew and try to persuade him to change or postpone the trip.
Talk to your sister and explain why you think she should reconsider her permission.
t6.note: Choose ONE option and speak to that person.
t6.model: Hey Leo, have you got a minute? I want to talk about the hiking trip, and I promise I’m not trying to ruin your summer. I think it’s great that you’re planning something like this yourselves. But I’ve been watching the fire maps, and that wildfire near the park has grown a lot in the last few days. Eighty kilometres sounds far, but with this wind and heat, fires can move surprisingly fast, and the smoke alone could make hiking pretty miserable. Plus, with the campfire ban, you won’t be able to cook the way you planned. Here’s my suggestion. What if you postponed it until September, when it’s cooler and the fire risk is lower? Or if you really want to go now, maybe pick a route closer to the highway with more exits. I’d even help you plan it and lend you my satellite messenger. What do you think?

t7.prompt: Some cities have decided that new homes and buildings can no longer be connected to natural gas, and must use electric heating and appliances instead. Do you think this is a good policy? Explain your reasons.
t7.model: In my opinion, banning natural gas connections in new buildings is a reasonable policy, as long as it’s introduced carefully. My first reason is timing. The easiest and cheapest moment to choose a heating system is when a building is being designed. If a new home is built with a gas furnace today, that furnace will probably run for twenty years, which means locking in emissions for decades. Retrofitting later is much more expensive and disruptive. Second, modern electric technology has improved enormously. Cold-climate heat pumps can now heat homes efficiently even in quite harsh winters, and induction stoves cook faster than gas and don’t release fumes into the kitchen, which is actually better for indoor air quality. That said, I understand the concerns. In some provinces, electricity is expensive, and people worry about losing heat during a power outage. Builders also say the rules could raise construction costs at a time when housing is already unaffordable. So I think governments should pair the policy with support, for example by making sure the electricity grid can handle the extra demand and requiring good insulation, so homes stay warm longer if the power goes out. Overall, though, I believe it’s a sensible step for new construction.

scene.alt: A backyard garden beside a small yellow house with a red roof. Growing in the garden are three gigantic flowers that are taller than the house itself, with huge colourful petals casting shade over the lawn. A white picket fence runs along the bottom of the yard. A woman in a pink dress stands next to the stems looking up, and a man in a blue shirt stands on a ladder against one stem, holding a camera. A wooden bench sits under the giant flowers, and a cat lies on the grass. There is a bright sun and one cloud.

t8.prompt: Your friend is getting married and is looking for an unusual garden for their outdoor wedding photos. You have found this garden. Call your friend, describe the garden, and explain whether you think it would be a good choice. Your friend cannot see the picture.
t8.model: Okay, you have to hear about this garden I just found for your photos. It’s behind a little yellow house with a red roof, and in the middle of the lawn there are three flowers that are honestly taller than the house. The petals are huge and brightly coloured, almost like giant umbrellas, and they throw this lovely shade over the grass. There’s a white picket fence along the bottom, a wooden bench right under the flowers, and even a sleepy cat on the lawn. When I was there, a photographer was up on a ladder taking shots from above. I really think it would be perfect. The pictures would look like something out of a fairy tale, and the shade means nobody would be squinting in the sun. My only worry is space, since it’s a fairly small yard, so it might work best for the couple and close family photos.
